page: Google Cloud Platform c4a-standard-16-lssd is an ARM-based server instance powered by the ARMv8 Neoverse-V2 architecture. It features 16 dedicated physical cores and 16 vCPUs, operating at a clock speed of 3.0 GHz with a single thread per core. The processor is equipped with 64 KB L1d cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 80 MB L3 cache. The system is configured with 64.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. For local storage, the instance includes 1608 GB of NVMe SSD capacity across four local drives. It does not include any GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data indicates strong memory subsystem performance, with the Passmark memory score placing in the top tier (top 10%). Large-block memory bandwidth tests show strong results in the top 25%, reaching 314.24 GB/sec for read-only and 120.6 GB/sec for write operations. CPU-bound benchmarks, such as single-threaded gzip compression and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, also perform in the top 25%. In database operations, the instance achieves a strong Passmark database score of 26,262.23. Standard compute benchmarks, including stress-ng and Passmark CPU tests, fall within the average range.

The instance offers high resource density and qualitative cost efficiency due to its dedicated ARM architecture and bundled high-capacity NVMe SSD storage. However, architectural tradeoffs include the absence of hyperthreading and lack of support for x86-specific vector extensions such as AVX, AVX512, or AMX. This makes the server less suitable for workloads relying on these instruction sets. Given its high-speed local storage and strong memory bandwidth, the c4a-standard-16-lssd is well-suited for database operations, software compilation, text and image processing, and general-purpose web serving.

Built on the ARMv8 architecture, it delivers strong memory performance, with its Passmark memory score reaching the top 10% tier and large-block memory bandwidth placing in the top 25%. While standard CPU benchmarks fall in the average range, the instance excels in single-threaded compression and database operations. Tradeoffs include a lack of hyperthreading and no support for AVX or AMX instruction sets. This configuration provides qualitative cost efficiency for I/O-heavy applications, making it highly suitable for database hosting, software compilation, text processing, and web serving workloads.
